text: Good evening. Good evening and welcome to the FY24 budget public hearing. On behalf of the school board I would like to thank you for taking time this evening to come and talk to us about the budget. We have one housekeeping item. Ms. Seismerheiser has submitted a written request to virtually attend this evening's public hearing due to a medical conflict. All those in favor of approving this request. Okay that is everyone here in attendance. Ms. Marin is absent this evening.

Tonight, 34 speakers have registered to address the board. When your name is called, in-person speakers should approach the podium and begin speaking, and virtual speakers should turn on their microphone and camera and begin speaking. Each speaker is allotted two minutes, and we ask that you stay within that time limit.

The school board welcomes community members to provide comments at its regular business meetings and public hearings on school board deliberations, school board-related issues, or particular topics. This evening, your remarks must address the FY24 budget.

If you have not registered to speak tonight, but would like an opportunity to address the board, please see the clerk to sign up for one of the five extra speaker slots. Your name will be called after the registered speakers have shared their comments.
Madame Clerk, please call our first speaker. - Our first speaker is student number one. - Good evening, ladies and gentlemen.

My name is Matt Heider, and I'm currently a senior at W.T. Woodson High School. I play football, lacrosse, and I wrestle, and I've done so for all four years. Before practices, you know, I'll have to visit the trainer and get stuff looked at, and we can't practice until we've been seen by the trainer, and sometimes this can take 30, 40 minutes, even an hour waiting.

And during football season, we can't practice until the trainer gets down to the field, and the trainer doesn't get down to the field until typically an hour 30 to two hours after school starts, which cuts a lot of time out of our practice schedule. When we have away games, the trainers will have to split time, and that just takes even more out of how much they can help us because there's only one trainer doing so.

And during the fall of my junior year, one of our starting defensive linemen got injured out of Saturday practice when we only had one trainer at the school. And he was up at the school instead of out the field during practice. And the player, Chris, happened to break his leg during practice.

and the trainer wasn't able to get down there until about 15 minutes after the injury occurred because he had to get everything good onto the field instead of having two trainers at the school and the trainer already being there.

My freshman year, we didn't have enough coverage from trainers and the one game where we had to borrow a trainer, we had seven concussions that game and the trainer wasn't familiar with us so they had trouble helping us out because they didn't know us.
Thank you. Thank you. Our next speaker is student number two. Hello, members of the Fairfax County School Board.

My name is Sarah Kate George, and I'm a junior at Lake Braddock, and I run track and play soccer for the school. I'm here to talk about obtaining a second full-time athletic trainer for all the high schools in FCPS. I've spent a lot of my time with the ATs at our school by playing two sports, and I also spend every other day in my sports medicine class that is taught by Miss A, our part-time athletic trainer.

I've learned a lot about the significance of having an athletic trainer at sporting events as well as hard as Miss A has to work. She comes in at school at 7 30 in the morning for her teaching job and usually doesn't leave until around 6 p.m. at the earliest and the occasional 9 10 and 11 p.m. depending on the sport. The part-time athletic trainers are only paid via stipend and without any benefits. I want to ensure that our athletic trainers in Fairfax County are not overworked to where they burn out and you have to find a new person to fill their position if anyone even applies for the position. Due to the current structure of pay and benefits for our part-time athletic trainers, they're forced to obtain a secondary job based on the cost of living

in Fairfax County. This requires them to spend, to split their attention and time and their responsibilities between the two positions. For our ATC2, Ms. A, she's also a teacher who has to grade lots of work, plan, and attend different meetings, all of outside of her athletic training duties. The part-time position is no longer appealing to the newer workforce of athletic trainers. When the compensation no longer aligns with the qualifications of these medical professionals, we are going to lose out on the quality of care that our student-athletes deserve. During the school year, the Lake Braddock athletic trainers have to care for

over 1,200 students per year. They can treat anywhere from 20 to 50 students every day. Based on guidelines created by the VDOE, every other job in the building has a student-to-employee ratio except for athletic trainers. They have no cap on how many students they can help, and it can become too much sometimes.
I have friends in other schools in Fairfax County and some of them only have one AT who has double the workload. Thank you. Your time is up. You finished your two minutes.
Thank you. Thank you. Our next speaker is student number three. Members of the school board, I appreciate the opportunity to address you here today.

My name is Ellie Sudarth and I am a junior at Lake Braddock Secondary on the girls lacrosse team. I'm here today to ask the board to consider funding a second full-time athletic trainer for every FCPS high school in the upcoming budget. The funding structure for the part-time athletic trainer position in Fairfax County high schools has remained unchanged since it was introduced in 1989.

The number of sports as well as the number of students participating in FCPS athletic programs has increased dramatically since that time. In the same breath, the roles, responsibilities, and quality of care our athletic trainers provide has evolved substantially since 1989.

For example, the care, monitoring, and rehabilitation of students, athletes suffering from a concussion has become much more extensive over the past 30 years. Most people have seen the recent news of the Buffalo Bills' safety to Mar Hamlin and his sudden collapse on the football field.

A Washington Post article dated January 10th, 2023, compared Hamlin's sudden cardiac arrest to that of Peter Lake, a Baltimore area high school lacrosse player, whose heart stopped when he was hit in the chest with a shot during a game. Lake was revived with an AED and made a full recovery, but as his father stated in the Washington Post article, If the trainer had been on the baseball field, Peter would not be here today.

My high school, Lake Braddock, like many others in Fairfax County, is a sprawling campus with numerous athletic facilities and playing fields. On any given night during the spring, you could have games on the softball, baseball, stadium fields, as well as the tennis courts, all at the same time. In the case of Peter Lake and DeMar Hamlin, tragedy was narrowly avoided because of the athletic trainers being able to provide care almost immediately.

To expect one full-time athletic trainer to provide immediate care across all athletic facilities is a disaster waiting to happen. Fairfax County is not only a top-notch school system, it is one of the greatest in the nation. And I hope you will all agree with me that the health and safety of our student-athletes should not be measured as an expense on a budget sheet, but as a top priority that is priceless.
Thank you. Our next speaker is student number four. Hello, my name is Alex Miller. I'm a student-athlete at Fairfax High School. I'm a junior.

I'm here to advocate for the funding of a second full-time athletic trainer. I'm a very injury-prone person. I'm in the trainer's clinic about as often as anybody. And there are many examples and stories I could give why it's helpful to me, very helpful.

Time, it saved me from having to see doctors, having doctors point them I didn't need to see. It saved me time from being referred to a specialist or knowing if something could actually be a serious problem. Like, once I had just a small cut, I didn't know it was infected, but luckily one of the trainers noticed it and it could have become something worse, something that was contagious, messing up a playoff run.

You obviously already know the importance of the trainers, but they already pointed out that there's no ratio of trainers to students. yet the student population in Fairfax County has increased by about 53,000 since the athletic trainer position structure has been established in 1989.

When our athletic leadership class found out that one of the trainers was part-time, it was very surprising, but most people were just frankly confused because both the trainers we have at Fairfax High School are very qualified, educated, hardworking people that we honestly talk about it regularly how hard-working and useful they are the fact that some schools are understaffed and don't have both athletic trainers was the craziest because it's something we see as a necessity like our like you was talking about earlier having both and readily accessible effects affects us

greatly and if you wish to advance athletics for the sake of students you also have to advance the assets they have to thank you our next speaker is student number five. Good evening members of the board. I want to thank you for letting me speak tonight. My name is Matt Norski. I am a senior at Woodson High School and I am a three-sport varsity athlete. It is because I'm a three-sport varsity athlete that I have seen my fair share of injuries and through these injuries I've gotten to meet the wonderful training staff

at Woodson High School and over the years I've gotten to meet them and it's just now coming to light how difficult their job has become. Currently there are three sports in season over the winter each of these sports have a girls team and a boys team each of these different categories have a varsity freshman and sophomore or a freshman JV and varsity level and we are putting the care of all these individuals in the hands of one person this is a huge workload that we are entrusting one person and it's easy to see how people can get burned out I've seen the line at the trainers go out the door and around the corner with kids

wanting to be seen about injuries they have acquired and to get taken care of so they can continue playing the game they love. With a second full-time trainer, we can have these athletes be seen twice as fast and assure quality care to not only us but the future of our sport programs.

Some trainers can have 14-hour days and their responsibilities have only been growing over the years. With the current pandemic, they have had to oversee COVID protocols, work multiple events in a single night, and these responsibilities have been growing exponentially.

We are seeing firsthand why FCPS is having a problem being fully staffed since 2014, because we are expecting one person to do the job of several. It's not fair to the individual, and it's not fair to the athletes who depend on that individual for recovery and rehabilitation. The last thing this athletic program needs is burned out, overworked trainers.

This is a recipe for disaster. Having only one trainer can have serious repercussions. For example, my school during the spring can have softball and lacrosse games at the same time. If a serious injury were to occur at one of these events and we did not have a trainer, we could see what happens. Thank you. Our next speaker is student number six.

Good afternoon. My name is Nicholas Romalo. I'm currently a senior at Fairfax High School and I've played soccer for all four years. I'm here to advocate for the funding of a second athletic trainer for full time at Fairfax County. Just like several other students, athletes at Fairfax High School have been lucky enough to have been treated by our athletic trainer assistant, Ms. Rhodes.

The point of Ms. Rose's position is obvious that when students found out of the 15,000 stipend that she gets, I got over 200 students that signed a global form in support of two full-time athletic trainers instead of a part-time. If they could, all 200 students would be here tonight.

Personally, Ms. Rose has helped me throughout the soccer season and even during the offseason for injuries such as small as turf burns, as big as a fractured finger. Seeing an average of about 40 to 60 student-athletes a day, depending on the season, shows the necessity of having a full-time athletic trainer assistant at all schools instead of just one full-time trainer. Thank you. Thank you. Our next speaker is Scott Peterson. Hi, my name is Scott Peterson and I'm vice chair of Faith Alliance for Climate Solutions. I want to thank you for

voting last year for the first of three multi-year initiatives to boost FCPS's environmental stewardship and I want to ask you to do it again this year by voting in favor of the year two initiatives. This is a critical step to fulfill recommendations from the Joint Environmental Task Force approved by the board in July of 2021. So we all know the story about the frog placed in water that's brought slowly to a boil, failing to perceive the danger until it's cooked to death.

Today, we as a society are that frog. Most days, the water doesn't seem that hot yet. Last year, over 6,000 communities in the U.S. broke all-time temperature records. Just this month, Scottsdale, Arizona stopped supplying water to a neighboring community because there's not enough going around.

According to Fairfax County government, very hot days at or above 95 degrees are projected to rise from seven days per year to more than 36 days a year in 2050. And by 2085, it's likely that most summer days will reach 95 degrees. Most young people, even if they don't know these facts, know what they're facing as they enter adulthood. In a recent survey of young people aged 16 to 25, 59% said they were extremely worried. They know the

water in the pot is heading to a boil. So that's why it's so important to show that you get it, that you're taking action on behalf of our students. We can turn down the temperature. Please vote for the year two budget initiatives. Thank you. Our next speaker is Elizabeth Endy. Good evening school board members and Superintendent Reed. My name

is Elizabeth Endy. I am also here as a member of FACTS to communicate the urgency of moving swiftly on climate action. Please vote in favor of the second year of the multi-year initiatives that enhance FCPS's environmental stewardship. I'd like to share my experience with Get to Green, which is one of the environmental programs slated for expansion this year. A decade ago, I met Elaine Tolan, the original Get to Green visionary, and attended meetings where schools across the county shared their environmental stewardship achievements. I always came away

from those meetings charged up, having seen firsthand how students learned problem-solving skills that would enable them to better take care of our earth. Resources from Get to Green were critical in helping the Longfellow Middle School student team that I worked with earn a National Wildlife Federation Green Flag Award.

The great thing is that the solutions students developed in school also made them better environmental stewards at home. Having a central group like Get to Green focused on developing, educating, and promoting best practices to all FCPS students and staff is key to meeting the important JET directives you approved in June 2021. It's a big job to reduce FCPS's carbon footprint and lead the way to ensuring a more sustainable environment. Thus, it is essential that the board fully fund the Get

to Green program and that FCPS promptly hire new staff to expand their ability to implement the program's critical goals. By continuing to fully engage with students, Get to Green will not only foster the development of young, dedicated environmental students, but it will enable all students' traditional AAP, ESOL, and special ed to become an in. Thank you. Our next speaker is Susan Stillman. Hi, my name is Susan Stillman. I'm a volunteer with the Virginia Chapter of the

Sierra Club. Thank you for the opportunity to speak this evening on the 2024 FCPS budget. I I spoke with an architect recently who does designs for FCPS and he said that they've been directed to no longer design to net zero because of the increases in the cost of construction.

I know something about that. I'm building a net zero home. If that's the case, then additional funds need to be acquired through a bond referendum. That needs to be on the 2023 bond if FCPS has any hope of meeting their commitments to going net zero.

As it relates to solar, there have been issues outside of FCPS's control that have obstructed the installation of solar, but these issues have been resolved, but yet the deployment is very slow. Only two schools have been approved by the board. I understand that a new process is being proposed which should expedite the installation of solar on FCPS schools.

That's great. But why is that a budget issue? Savings that will be garnered through deploying solar can be folded back into operating funds. It's also a budget issue because the monopoly utility from which you all buy most of your electricity is in the General Assembly right now trying to prop up their stock price by locking in their profits.

If they're successful, they're going to pass those increases on to you all and to me, to everybody. We've got to lock in the price of energy by installing solar. You'll know what your costs are for the next 20 years. also passing on the increases in fossil gas right that they use as a fuel to generate electricity so if we don't get the solar installed we're going to have a lot of regret because we're paying a lot more than we need to for electricity we can't roll back the clock but

let's get moving thank you thank you our next speaker is amy lacrosse hi my name is amy lacrosse and I am an Elementary Special Education Department Chair. First, I would like to thank Dr. Reed and the board for their support of the $2 million earmarked in the budget proposal for the Special Education Compensatory Services Fund.

This amount is necessary, though likely inadequate, to meet the requirements of the OCR settlement. I would also like to acknowledge the continuation of the eight-hour contract for special education teachers and how, while insufficient, it provides much-needed acknowledgement of the incredible workload of our special education staff.

Thank you, Dr. Reed, for prioritizing staff compensation and support. I do, however, feel the need to highlight that bonuses are short-term commitments that take away from long-term solutions. We need salary increases over highly taxed bonuses. Is FCPS aware of what neighboring counties are providing in an effort to retain highly qualified staff?

In reviewing the budget proposal, I was struck by the multi-year investment of $1.6 million in funding to carry out the recommendations of the AAP external review. I don't understand why similar funding requests are not included in response to the AIR special education audit.

The 19 recommendations in that report are clear, actionable, and would greatly improve special education if implemented as written. Instead of simply funding implementation of these recommendations, FCPS has chosen to proceed with a confusing and drawn-out process involving multiple committees whose makeup is not publicly known. Several of these recommendations largely concern teacher support. However, DSS decided to consolidate recommendations into four areas, none of which directly support our teachers. The Special Education Enhancement Plan Steering Committee has now been told that it will not write goals, but will instead review goals created by

staff. These may or may not match the clear recommendations the researchers in the AIR review offered after two years of careful study. This is puzzling. Please explain why the AAP external review resulted in direct funding of those recommendations. Thank you. Our next speaker is Anne Marie O'Donnell. Good evening and thank you for the opportunity to address the school board.

My name is Anne Marie O'Donnell and I currently have one child attending Hayfield Elementary School with two others waiting in the wind. When my husband received his final assignment in the Army, we made the deliberate decision to move to Fairfax County rather than remain in Maryland. We based our decision in no small part on Fairfax County Public School's great reputation.

FCPS has the reputation for being the best in the nation. That is a reputation every teacher, administrator, board member, and principal should be proud of and in passion to continue. Overall, our experience at Hayfield has been positive. Our son Jack thrives there and has dreams of becoming a NASA engineer one day.

He is fascinated by all things science and yearns to be challenged. Science and math are by far his favorite subjects, and on any given Sunday, He will be watching YouTube videos, watching Mark Rober demonstrating principles of engineering or learning about galaxy. He loves his STEM classes and so do all of his friends.

We are at a pivotal moment in our nation's history. Technological evolutions have and will continue to change science fiction into science fact and along with it the world. As technology evolves, our children's education, especially in the STEM fields, is increasingly important. The U.S. was once the world's leader in technological innovation, however, we are falling further and further behind.

We quite literally shot for the moon and landed. We created the internet, cell phones, smartphones, and life-saving vaccines. American ingenuity has changed the world and saved people's lives. From President Biden down to Supervisor Lusk, every single elected leader knows and agrees the importance of STEM education.

Every single responsible parent in America agrees on the importance of STEM in their children's education. Fairfax County Public Schools openly takes pride in its STEM education across the country. Their number one school is a STEM school whose kids just put a satellite into space. So imagine my surprise when I recently found out that our STEM program, our part-time, our teacher is not only a part-time teacher now due to budget cuts, but that we are in danger of losing our STEM program altogether.

I stand here today and ask you why this is even a consideration. I ask that you continue to invest in our children's future by giving them the tools needed to be successful on the world stage by continuing to fund STEM in our schools and increase our budget. Thank you.

Our next speaker is Emily Vanderhoff. Good evening, Dr. Reed, Budget Chair Tolan, and members of the board. My name is Emily Vanderhoff. I'm a first grade teacher in FCPS and a proud member of my union, FCFT.

I first want to thank Dr. Reed for prioritizing staff compensation in her proposed budget. I hope that the board will keep the step and 3% MSA in the advertised budget and advocate to the Board of Supervisors to fully fund the transfer. I would also like to advocate that you consider taking the funds budgeted for the retention bonus and applying it towards the salary scale to ensure that a greater portion of the investment goes directly to employees since bonuses are highly taxed.

As an elementary teacher, I'm glad to see the parity with secondary staff in compensation for leadership roles. There are a lot of extra roles that educators are asked to take on, usually with no compensation. So I hope this is the first step in recognizing additional leadership responsibilities with appropriate compensation.

I also support increasing pay at the top of the scale to promote retention. I understand that when the scale was revised in 2016 and shortened to 23 steps, the maximum salary at the time was moved to Step 23 to put employees at their highest pay sooner. It seems that over time, the counties with more steps have far outpaced our highest pay, and in the FY23 Way-B report, our maximum teacher pay ranks eighth out of nine in comparison to surrounding districts.

Additionally, those at the top of the scale express feeling unvalued when their pay stays stagnant for up to 10 years before they're eligible to retire, making these employees consider leaving FCPS before planned. I hope the board can further research how to best balance honoring experience while also ensuring staff can all reach their highest pay. I'm also glad that special education contract will remain in FY24 with ESSER funds and I hope that the board keeps this budget item in mind in future budgets when ESSER funds are discontinued. I always say that for everything that I have to do as classroom teacher, my teachers have to do ten times more and so I fully support this

being a continuing item in future budgets. Thank you for your consideration. thank you our next speaker is Cheryl Hyder good evening my name is Cheryl Hyder thank you first for the opportunity to address you all this evening we do appreciate sincerely everything that you guys are doing to give our kids safety and well-being the fourth you know the foremost thought coming out of COVID I think we all appreciated its importance just a little bit

more than perhaps we did prior tonight I want to talk to you about risk not the risk that continuing without two full-time trainers at each school you know will cause more staffing difficulties for these positions I'm going to leave that to others to address with you instead I want to talk about managing the risks associated with participation in high school athletics overall and that's the risk of physical injury so now parents complete paperwork to confirm kids are healthy they're able to participate probably also sign a waiver of liability so fine you all have addressed the legal risk that covers the school it does not

cover the kids. Not having the right resources, meaning the two full-time trainers who are not overwhelmed and who instead are able to focus on the athlete's care and feeding, the county essentially is taking a passive reactive approach to ensuring their safety in these activities.

For example, at Woodson, our trainers in the past three seasons saw 500 individual activities or injuries, excuse me, requiring care end-to-end, you know, rehab and putting them back on the field if they you know if they were able to that's in addition to the assorted bumps bruises you know and sadness you know triaging the incident immediate care coordinating with the athlete's doctor or parent or coach overseeing rehab coordinated coordinating the agreed upon return to play then you have to worry about hurting the kids onto and off of the field did I mention the
seven concussions in one freshman football game what if that game was deprioritized because they

were only freshmen and we had no trainer there. What would that have done? Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you very much. Our next speaker is Misha Chernov. Good evening Madam Chair school board members and Dr. Reed. My name is Misha Chernov. I'm an FCPS teacher and resident. Thank you for the opportunity to speak tonight regarding the FY24 proposed budget. I wish I could say this budget gives me confidence in the direction and future of Fairfax County public schools. But unfortunately

it does not. Here are three reasons why I feel this budget comes up short. First a 3% MRA is not enough. It's simply not enough to keep up with the current rate of inflation. Second we have been telling you that we don't have enough teacher directed planning time. We don't have enough substitutes which means we find ourselves covering classes at the last minute thus losing the planning time we already don't have enough of. This budget does not address these issues. Third

Health care. In my 27 years of employment with FCPS, I never once worried about having access to high quality health care at a reasonable cost. Until now. Colleagues of mine are learning that their current physicians do not accept Cigna and have told them they will not join the Cigna network.

While I understand the division will be saving $70 to $90 million over the course of the five-year contract with Cigna, I am fully aware that this is coming at the expense of your employees, who will now have greater out-of-pocket costs with fewer health care providers in the Cigna network.

There is no amount of spin or positive reframing from the division leadership team that can deny this truth. Before I leave, I want to share that I am opposed to funding school officers in elementary schools under the data-less pretense that it will help keep students safe.
Direct this funding to school counselors, social workers, and psychologists. Our students need those safety supports. Thank you. Thank you. Our next speaker is Robert Rigby. Good evening.

My name is Robert Rigby. I am an employee in my 40th year as an educator. Tonight, I speak for myself and do not represent the views of any organization. Budget is policy. How we spend our money affects children, family visitors, and staff safety.

Some families at Waples Mill Elementary have asked me to relay a serious appeal for help around addressing a grave increase in worrisome incidents at their school. These concerns are similar to those around the county, state, and nation.

My friends tell me they are truly serious at Waipos Mill. Note, they do not relay concerns that this is because of inclusion or teacher leniency, and they seem unrelated to that dreadful three strikes HB 1461 brought in the General Assembly.

But it is a major uptick in incidents. The incidents include lockdowns, intruders, sexual harassment and assault, and serious threats. They express for themselves feeling left out on the ground for security because they're known as a quiet, peaceful background.

They say they no longer are. They ask specifically for vestibules, cameras, better locks, and increased monitors to pay attention to outdoor places where children may be at risk. Thank you for listening. Thank you. Our next speaker is Deborah Vincent.
Hello, everyone, the board. My name is Debbie Vincent. I'm here to support the funding for every Fairfax County public school high school to have two full-time athletic trainers.

So that I'm not repeating what you've already heard, I'm just going to dive into my family's experiences with Ms. K, the full-time AT, and Ms. A, the part-time AT, and who happens to be a full-time teacher at Lake Braddock. My son, Dom, is a senior varsity football player, and I can't begin to describe how crucial both ATs were for Dom.

Dom had numerous injuries over the years, including a torn ACL, two concussions, and a hamstring tear. Each injury was tended to by both ATs in a tag team effort, because other players needed help too. In fact, when my son tore his ACL on a Thursday, it was the AT, Ms. K, who was able to get him an appointment the very next morning with the team's surgeon.

During Dom's recovery, once COVID hit and his PT got shut down, Ms. K would meet us outside in a park to make sure that his injury was healed correctly. I have personally observed both ATs evaluating injuries, providing treatments, and rehab services, and providing game coverage.

The importance of having a highly educated, trained, and caring AT at all events is crucial to the health and well-being of not only students, but everyone in attendance. You never know when someone might sprain an ankle, tear an ACL, get a concussion, or God forbid, suffer cardiac arrest like we all saw with the NFL.

We owe it to all Fairfax County students to have an appropriate number of athletic trainers available and on staff. I hope you can support this crucial need and allocate funding for a second full-time athletic trainer in the upcoming budget. Thank you.
- Thank you. Our next speaker is Andrea Edelstein. - Good evening, Superintendent Reed, Budget Chair Tallinn, and members of the school board.

I appreciate the opportunity to speak to you tonight to voice my support for prioritizing student safety by allocating funding in this 2024 budget for two full-time athletic trainers for each Fairfax County high school and secondary school. My name is Andrea Edelstein.

I'm the parent of two FCPS students, a senior and a junior. My junior is a member of the Lake Braddock football team where I am an active volunteer. I also serve on the board of our athletic booster club. Those roles have given me the opportunity to get to know our athletic trainers and learn more about what they do to enhance safety for our student athletes and others.

Many naively think that the extent of an athletic trainer's role is to tape injuries on the sidelines of a game. That does not even begin to scratch the surface of what they do. During 2020, our athletic trainers put protocols in place that allowed us to safely train during quarantine. In addition to being really good at what they do, they also have a great rapport with our student-athletes and coaches, which puts athletes at ease when they're in situations where they need their support and guidance.

Our athletic trainers are our unsung heroes that many people don't really know about until or unless their kids face serious injuries. Athletic trainers are required to have a master's degree from an accredited program, national certification, and be medically licensed to practice in Virginia, yet the current stipend pay structure does not align with payment for such qualified medical professionals.

This impacts the ability to attract, hire, and retain athletic trainers to keep our students safe. While Virginia Department of Education has standards of quality ratios for most other positions, there are no such standards for our athletic trainers, who in a year may work with over 1,200 student-athletes, evaluate more than 1,600 injuries, and provide over 6,000 treatments.

On many nights, the school might have multiple events going on. Our athletic trainer cannot be at the stadium and in the gym simultaneously. If a critical injury were to occur, response time is key, and the trainer would need to be notified and get from the stadium to the gym, costing valuable time.
But the issue goes beyond coverage at events. Thank you. Thank you. Our next speaker is Dawn Martinez. Thank you, and good evening. You've heard a lot of this already. I'll try to go fast.

Athletic trainers are nationally certified, state-licensed medical professionals. They are a necessary component to any athletic department, especially the programs caring for our student athletes. A master's degree, a national certification, and a state medical license are required for all ATs.

Whether they're the main AT or the associate AT, they both need these same requirements. At FCPS, we are compensating our associate ATs at an annual stipend of merely $16,398, and that comes without any benefits at all.

And I know you all know that already. They are paid probably less than $10 an hour by the time you factor in all of the hours they work beyond what they're expected to work. And we know that we need this for our student athletes to be safe and cared for when we have so much division of so many different athletic contests at the same time.

I'm a parent since 2008 with Fairfax County Public Schools. My son is now wrestling in college. My daughter is a junior at South County High School, where she is also a triple athlete. We have been blessed to see a program with both trainer positions filled, and now we are one of the seven with only one trainer.

The difference has gone almost unnoticed, but you can see the difference when you look at Ms. H's face. And the division and the pull in each different direction, I really hope that when you are looking this year to fund compensation to attract and retain you consider not only attracting a full-time at for every second position at every school but consider that you will also be retaining

thank you our next speaker is emily yewens hello my name is emily ewens and i'm a class of 2022 Lake Braddock graduate. I was a student athlete at Lake Braddock, which is how I met our athletic trainers. My sophomore year, they encouraged me to join their athletic training student aid program where I could observe their duties day in and day out. I learned how to assess and treat athletes and helped out in any way that I could. After three years of enriching high school experience, I was inspired to sign up for the sports medicine student aid program at Virginia Tech this semester.

Because of the relationship I have built with our ITs, I feel I have a unique perspective on why it's so important to fund a second full-time athletic training position for all FCPS high schools.
